figures.caption: Left: FlashAttention uses tiling to prevent materialization of the large $N\times N$ attention matrix (dotted box) on (relatively) slow GPU HBM. In the outer loop (red arrows), FlashAttention loops through blocks of the $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ matrices and loads them to fast on-chip SRAM. In each block, FlashAttention loops over blocks of $\mathbf{Q}$ matrix (blue arrows), loading them to SRAM, and writing the output of the attention computation back to HBM. citing_sentences: In this paper, we argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware [1]—that is, carefully accounting for reads and writes to different levels of fast and slow memory (e.g., between fast GPU on-chip SRAM and relatively slow GPU high bandwidth memory, or HBM [45], Figure 1 left).

Even with the increased FLOPs due to recomputation, our algorithm both runs faster (up to 7.6x on GPT-2 [67], Figure 1 right) and uses less memory—linear in sequence length—than standard attention, thanks to the massively reduced amount of HBM access.

abstract: Transformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in sequence length. Approximate attention methods have attempted to address this problem by trading off model quality to reduce the compute complexity, but often do not achieve wall-clock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware—accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU memory. We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity of FlashAttention, showing that it requires fewer HBM accesses than standard attention, and is optimal for a range of SRAM sizes. We also extend FlashAttention to block-sparse attention, yielding an approximate attention algorithm that is faster than any existing approximate attention method. FlashAttention trains Transformers faster than existing baselines: 15% end-to-end wall-clock speedup on BERT-large (seq. length 512) compared to the MLPerf 1.1 training speed record, 3$\times$ speedup on GPT-2 (seq. length 1K), and 2.4$\times$ speedup on long-range arena (seq. length 1K-4K). FlashAttention and block-sparse FlashAttention enable longer context in Transformers, yielding higher quality models (0.7 better perplexity on GPT-2 and 6.4 points of lift on long-document classification) and entirely new capabilities: the first Transformers to achieve better-than-chance performance on the Path-X challenge (seq. length 16K, 61.4% accuracy) and Path-256 (seq. length 64K, 63.1% accuracy).

sections.body: The section argues that the missing principle is making attention IO-aware, meaning it counts reads and writes between fast on-chip SRAM and slower HBM. FlashAttention uses tiling and fuses attention into one CUDA kernel. It computes exact attention with memory linear in sequence length and runs up to 7.6x faster on GPT-2 attention. The IO analysis shows up to 9x fewer HBM accesses than standard attention. A lower bound shows no exact algorithm asymptotically improves on these accesses over all SRAM sizes. Block-sparse FlashAttention is 2-4x faster than FlashAttention and scales to sequence length 64k. Reported training speedups are 15% on BERT-large, 3x on GPT-2, and 2.4x on long-range arena.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Attention is quadratic in sequence length, and making it IO-aware reduces slow GPU memory accesses while keeping results exact.

sections.body: The section describes GPU memory. An A100 has 40-80GB of HBM at 1.5-2.0TB/s and 192KB of on-chip SRAM per each of 108 streaming multiprocessors. The SRAM is about an order of magnitude faster than HBM but many orders of magnitude smaller. Operations are compute-bound or memory-bound, and softmax, dropout and layer norm are memory-bound. Kernel fusion reduces repeated reads, but training still writes intermediate values to HBM. Standard attention materializes the score and probability matrices in HBM, which takes O(N²) memory. The section notes that N is often much larger than d, for example N=1024 and d=64 for GPT-2.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: GPU attention is memory-bound, and standard attention writes the N by N score and probability matrices to HBM.

sections.body: The method splits Q, K and V into blocks loaded from HBM into SRAM and combines block results using softmax statistics, so the N by N matrix is never stored. The backward pass recomputes attention on-chip from the saved output and normalization statistics. Theorem 2 gives Θ(N²d²M⁻¹) HBM accesses for FlashAttention against Θ(Nd+N²) for standard attention, when d ≤ M ≤ Nd. Proposition 3 says no exact algorithm uses o(N²d²M⁻¹) HBM accesses for all M in that range. Block-sparse FlashAttention costs Θ(Nd+N²d²M⁻¹s), where s is the fraction of nonzero blocks. Figure 2 shows runtime follows HBM access counts. The authors leave parameterized lower bounds in terms of M as future work.
sections.heading: FlashAttention: Algorithm, Analysis, and Extensions
sections.headline: Tiling and recomputation give exact attention with fewer HBM accesses, and a lower bound limits any exact algorithm.

sections.body: Table 1 reports BERT-large training to 72.0% masked language modeling accuracy in 17.4 ± 1.4 minutes with FlashAttention, against 20.0 ± 1.5 minutes for the Nvidia MLPerf 1.1 implementation. Results average 10 runs on 8 A100 GPUs. Table 2 shows GPT-2 medium training in 6.9 days with FlashAttention, against 21.0 days for HuggingFace and 11.5 days for Megatron-LM. Table 3 shows FlashAttention reaches an average of 59.8 on long-range arena against 59.3 for the standard Transformer, with a 2.4x speedup. Table 4 shows GPT-2 small at context length 4k is 30% faster than Megatron-LM at 1k, with 0.7 better perplexity.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: FlashAttention trains BERT-large 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record and GPT-2 up to 3x faster than HuggingFace.

sections.body: The section names three limitations. Each new attention implementation currently requires a new kernel written in a lower-level language than PyTorch, which takes significant engineering effort. Implementations may not transfer across GPU architectures. The authors suggest compiling high-level attention code to IO-aware kernels, similar to Halide for image processing. They also say the IO-aware approach may extend beyond attention to other modules. The implementation is optimal within constants for a single GPU. The IO analysis does not yet account for data transfer between multiple GPUs.
sections.heading: Limitations and Future Directions
sections.headline: Limitations are that each attention variant needs its own low-level GPU kernel and that multi-GPU data transfer is not analyzed.

sections.body: Appendix A reviews IO-aware runtime optimization, structured matrices, sparse training and efficient Transformers. Appendix B derives the forward and backward passes with linear extra memory and gives the full FlashAttention algorithms. Proofs of the IO results are in Appendix C. Appendix D discusses extensions of IO-aware methods beyond attention. Appendix E contains further experiment details, GPT-2 validation curves, and full runtime and memory tables for exact, approximate and sparse baselines across sequence lengths from 128 to 65536.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, backward-pass derivations, algorithm details, proofs, extensions and full benchmark tables.
